domain_assessment.domain: Industrial process engineering, surface-treatment qualification, and automotive-style PPAP quality approval
domain_assessment.role: Process engineer responsible for qualifying surface treatment on new anodizing equipment
domain_assessment.objective: Identify and mitigate the contributors to intermittent aluminum-bracket micro-pitting quickly enough to support a clean validation lot and timely PPAP submission
domain_assessment.incident_type: Intermittent micro-pitting defect on aluminum brackets produced by a new anodizing line, with potential temperature, rectifier, chemistry-control, material, and handling contributors

decision_points.summary: Initial defect investigation: prioritizing a temperature explanation and attributing a day-shift defect-rate gap
evidence_before: Night-shift operator handoff note reporting an overnight bath-temperature spike
A short rectifier-log summary in the same folder flagging a calibration deviation from several days earlier
Day-shift versus night-shift defect-rate report
Unreviewed coil chemistry certificates
Prior observation that the newer day-shift operator sometimes rushed rack loading
evidence_after: Pitting declined but did not disappear
Residual pitting was treated as more consistent with chemistry-control variation
goals_constraints: Run a clean trial lot before PPAP submission
Operate under approximately three weeks of remaining schedule slack
alternatives: Prioritize temperature-controller and chiller diagnostics
Open and investigate the rectifier calibration-deviation summary
Review incoming coil chemistry certificates
Investigate shift-specific equipment or chemistry drift
Treat operator rack-loading behavior as a possible contributor
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly states that the first temperature explanation became the frame for the investigation and caused the rectifier summary to remain unopened despite its availability.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: the issue emerged about three weeks before a customer PPAP submission.
decision_points.uncertainty: Several technically plausible causes existed, and the temperature issue was later shown to be only a partial explanation.

decision_points.summary: Selection of a corrective dosing-control technology between Vendor A and Vendor B
evidence_before: Vendor A retrofit was installed at three sister plants
Two sister-plant engineers reported generally favorable experiences with Vendor A
One of the three Vendor A plants had mixed results
Vendor B had stronger specifications on the sensing and control criteria considered most important
Vendor B had one reference installation and incomplete installation and commissioning documentation
An incomplete requirement-by-requirement comparison was initially favoring Vendor B technically
Vendor B's applications engineer offered support to clarify commissioning gaps
No Vendor B incompatibility had been identified
evidence_after: Vendor A was selected and installed within three days
The requirement-by-requirement comparison was not completed
Vendor B's offered commissioning clarification was not pursued
goals_constraints: Choose a technically viable option under a compressed implementation schedule
alternatives: Select Vendor A based on existing sister-plant use
Select Vendor B based on stronger technical sensing and control criteria
Complete the requirement-by-requirement comparison before selecting
Use Vendor B's applications-engineering support to resolve open commissioning questions
Delay selection pending additional implementation evidence
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant stopped an evaluation that was favoring Vendor B after learning that three sister plants used Vendor A, and separately rejected Vendor B because unresolved documentation gaps felt less acceptable than Vendor A's familiar unknowns.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: corrective technology had to be implemented quickly enough to preserve the PPAP schedule.
decision_points.uncertainty: Vendor B had stronger known technical attributes but less established implementation evidence; Vendor A had broader internal adoption but at least one mixed reference outcome.

decision_points.summary: Interpreting the post-retrofit batch sequence and assigning causal credit for apparent improvement
evidence_before: Vendor A retrofit installation
Two early post-installation batches with minor pitting
Five subsequent clean batches
Routine bath-chemistry replenishment during the same period
Manual rectifier-voltage adjustments made by the participant between runs
An incomplete SPC sample relative to the normal stability threshold
evidence_after: Certification paperwork preparation began in parallel with further process observation
The participant did not declare the process stable
The participant later acknowledged that the manual-adjustment and replenishment effects had never been separated
goals_constraints: Assess whether the process trajectory was improving
Avoid prematurely declaring a process stable before the recommended SPC sample was complete
alternatives: Treat the clean streak as evidence that bad outcomes had been statistically offset or used up
Treat the clean streak as provisional while continuing SPC sampling
Attribute improvement primarily to the retrofit
Attribute improvement primarily to the chemistry replenishment
Attribute improvement primarily to manual voltage adjustments
Avoid causal attribution until the competing factors were separated
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant interpreted the clean streak as if earlier bad luck or instability had been used up, while separately crediting personal manual voltage adjustments more than a concurrent bath-chemistry replenishment.
decision_points.time_pressure: High: documentation activity had to begin before the full recommended sample size could be obtained.
decision_points.uncertainty: The batch sequence occurred amid multiple concurrent changes, and the participant explicitly maintained that formal process-stability judgment remained open.

evidence_before: A two-week trial dataset containing meaningful variability in earlier lots
A clean final validation lot completed one day before submission
A marginal Cpk finding from a quality audit
A 24-hour deadline for the customer SQE sign-off memo
evidence_after: Earlier trial data were referenced but given less weight
The separately filed marginal Cpk finding was not made central in the recommendation
goals_constraints: Provide the SQE with a timely sign-off memo
Balance schedule risk against unresolved process-capability uncertainty
alternatives: Weight the full two-week dataset and marginal Cpk result heavily
Treat the final validation lot as one observation within the wider evidence base
Delay submission or make the recommendation conditional
Give the most recent clean lot primary weight in recommending certification
decision_points.decision_basis: The participant explicitly treated the latest clean validation lot as the truest representation of current process state and assigned it most of the weight in the certification recommendation.
decision_points.time_pressure: Very high: the customer SQE required the sign-off memo within 24 hours.
decision_points.uncertainty: The final lot was favorable but represented one observation against a fuller historical dataset that contained earlier variability and a marginal capability indication.

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: There was actually a short rectifier-log summary sitting in the same folder that flagged a calibration deviation from a few days earlier, but I didn't open it that week — the temperature story was already the frame I was working from, so the chiller took priority and the rectifier note just sat there.
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 1; initial investigation account following the temperature-spike handoff note
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The first-attended diagnostic explanation, the reported temperature spike, becomes the participant's working frame and receives disproportionate attention over a competing rectifier-deviation cue that was available at the same time. The later counterfactual probe confirms that review order itself shaped hypothesis prioritization.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Temperature is a familiar, actionable, and genuinely plausible pitting contributor, so checking it first can be legitimate diagnostic triage. The occurrence is nevertheless supported because the participant says the initial temperature story became the frame and left a flagged competing diagnostic summary unopened for the week.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required. The available competing rectifier evidence, attention-allocation behavior, explicit framing language, and review-order counterfactual together make the mechanism identifiable.

revision.location: Decision point 1; participant explanation of the unopened rectifier summary
revision.current_defect: None material. The episode identifies a first-attended explanation, an available competing cue, delayed competing-evidence review, and the participant's own description of framing.
preserve: The temperature report as the first-attended explanation
The rectifier summary's availability in the same folder
The rectifier calibration deviation as a plausible competing diagnostic cue
The counterfactual that changes only evidence-review order
avoid_creating: Do not add active search for temperature-confirming data that would create a separate confirmation-bias occurrence
Do not make the rectifier deviation conclusively establish the true root cause
Do not merge the investigation-prioritization episode with the operator-attribution episode

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: Honestly, my first instinct was that the day-shift operator was less careful — he's newer, and I'd noticed him rushing rack loading a couple times... I didn't spend much time asking whether the equipment was in worse condition during the day, or whether the chemistry itself might drift over the course of a shift. I focused on him.

target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant assigns a shift-level performance difference primarily to a person's care and behavior while acknowledging that plausible situational explanations, including equipment condition and chemistry drift, were available but not seriously investigated.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Observed rushed rack loading could genuinely contribute to defects, so considering operator performance is not itself biased. The occurrence is supported because the participant prematurely privileged the dispositional explanation while not seriously assessing credible situational and process-level alternatives.

revision.current_defect: None material. The transcript contains a distinct causal-attribution act, a dispositional explanation, and explicitly neglected situational alternatives.
preserve: The operator's newer status and observed rushing
The day-shift defect-rate gap
The participant's failure to seriously investigate equipment and chemistry alternatives
Separation from the primacy episode through different evidence and reasoning operations
avoid_creating: Do not add conclusive evidence that the operator actually caused the defects
Do not convert the episode into a general quality-control failure rather than an attribution judgment

target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: Vendor B's applications engineer even offered to walk us through the open commissioning questions, and there wasn't any identified incompatibility, but the unresolved gaps still felt less acceptable to me than Vendor A's familiar unknowns, so I didn't take him up on it.
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 2; participant explanation of Vendor B elimination
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant avoids Vendor B despite its stronger known sensing and control attributes, available clarification support, and no identified incompatibility because unresolved information feels less acceptable than familiar uncertainty associated with Vendor A.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Incomplete documentation and limited reference installations are legitimate implementation risks in a deadline-constrained manufacturing project. The occurrence is supported because the participant does not pursue available clarification, identifies no incompatibility, and explicitly contrasts aversion to unresolved gaps with acceptance of Vendor A's familiar unknowns.

revision.location: Decision point 2; Vendor B documentation and applications-engineering support response

preserve: Vendor B's stronger sensing and control criteria
Vendor B's incomplete documentation and one-reference-installation context
The availability of Vendor B applications-engineering support

The distinction from Vendor A peer-adoption evidence

Do not use sister-plant adoption as the primary evidence in this episode

But once I had three sister plants confirming Vendor A worked, that was enough for me — I didn't finish walking through the rest of the comparison.

target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Sister-plant deployments and practitioner feedback are relevant implementation evidence, particularly under time pressure. target_occurrence_audit.supporting_quote: Honestly, after those two rough batches, having five clean ones in a row felt like the process had settled the score — like whatever bad luck or instability had been in the system early on had been used up, so another rough batch felt a lot less likely right then.
target_occurrence_audit.evidence_location: Decision point 3; participant interpretation of two defective post-retrofit batches followed by five clean batches
target_occurrence_audit.mechanism: The participant treats earlier unfavorable outcomes as having been used up or statistically offset by later clean outcomes, and therefore treats another bad batch as less likely because of the preceding sequence. This is compensatory sequence reasoning rather than a process-capability assessment.
target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: Batch outcomes in a manufacturing system can be serially dependent because process conditions may genuinely change after a retrofit, replenishment, or adjustment. The occurrence remains supported because the participant explicitly invokes bad luck or instability being used up and describes the sequence as having settled the score, rather than citing controlled evidence of an improved process state.
target_occurrence_audit.additional_evidence_needed: None required for the occurrence as written. The participant's explicit compensatory framing supplies the required mechanism.

revision.location: Decision point 3; batch-sequence interpretation immediately after the five clean batches
revision.current_defect: None material. The participant provides explicit compensatory reasoning tied to chronological outcomes and separately states that formal stability judgment remained open.

target_occurrence_audit.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The manual voltage adjustments may have contributed materially to the improvement. The occurrence is supported because the participant claims primary personal causal credit without evidence capable of separating that action from the concurrent chemistry intervention or other process changes.

It was the cleanest result we'd seen, run right before submission, so it felt like the truest picture of where the process actually stood. additional_candidate_biases.bias: Law of small numbers / premature stability inference
additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: We started prepping the certification paperwork in parallel because the timeline demanded it, not because I was ready to call the process stable — I was still treating that call as open.
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: A possible concern would be treating a five-batch clean streak as sufficient evidence of stability before reaching the normal SPC sample size.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The participant expressly distinguishes administrative certification preparation from a stability determination, says the stability call remained open, and attributes the paperwork timing to the calendar rather than to the streak. This is deadline-driven parallel work, not a separate premature-stability occurrence.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: The temperature story was already the frame I was working from, so the chiller took priority and the rectifier note just sat there.
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The initial framing could superficially resemble selective evidence processing.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The transcript does not show active search for temperature-confirming evidence, distortion of contradictory evidence, or persistence in the temperature hypothesis after pitting persisted. It more specifically supports primacy-driven initial prioritization.

additional_candidate_biases.supporting_quote: Another rough batch felt a lot less likely right then... given the run we'd had.
additional_candidate_biases.mechanism: The most recent clean streak is treated as predictive of continued clean performance.
additional_candidate_biases.plausible_nonbias_explanation: The explicit operative reasoning is compensatory: earlier bad luck or instability had been used up and the process had settled the score. That is more directly captured by Gambler's Fallacy than by a distinct hot-hand occurrence. Counting both would duplicate the same reasoning episode.

nonbias_cues.cue: Investigating the reported temperature spike promptly.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Bath temperature is described as a known and easily checked pitting contributor, and temperature stabilization was followed by a partial reduction in defects. Prompt investigation is rational triage; the bias lies specifically in leaving a flagged competing rectifier cue unopened because the first explanation became the frame.

nonbias_cues.cue: Updating away from a temperature-only explanation after residual pitting persists.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant revises the initial causal model after the chiller repair fails to eliminate pitting. This is evidence of appropriate updating rather than a separate confirmation or perseverance bias.

nonbias_cues.cue: Considering rushed operator rack loading as one potential contributor.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Observed handling behavior can be relevant to surface-treatment defects. The bias is not the consideration of behavior itself, but the disproportionate dispositional attribution without comparable investigation of situational alternatives.

nonbias_cues.cue: Using sister-plant reference-site experience in vendor selection.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Reference deployments and direct reports from comparable plants can be valid evidence about implementation, reliability, and commissioning. The bandwagon occurrence is supported only because the participant lets adoption prevalence terminate a technically relevant comparison that was favoring Vendor B.

nonbias_cues.cue: Concern about Vendor B's incomplete documentation and limited reference base.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Sparse installation documentation and unclear commissioning processes are genuine implementation risks. The ambiguity-effect occurrence arises because clarification support was available, no incompatibility was identified, and the participant still preferred familiar unknowns over unresolved but potentially resolvable uncertainty.

nonbias_cues.cue: Beginning certification paperwork before the complete SPC sample is available.
nonbias_cues.location: Decision point 3; response to the SPC sample-size question
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant explicitly says that formal stability judgment remained open and that parallel documentation work was driven by the calendar. The action therefore reflects schedule management rather than a distinct unsupported claim that the process was statistically stable.

nonbias_cues.cue: The marginal Cpk result was filed separately from the sign-off packet.
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: Separate filing is an organizational-information condition. It does not independently establish a cognitive bias; the recency effect is supported by the participant's subsequent choice to give the latest lot most of the evidentiary weight.

nonbias_cues.cue: The participant retrospectively acknowledges that reviewing the rectifier deviation first might have changed the initial investigation.
nonbias_cues.location: Counterfactual probe near the close of the interview
nonbias_cues.why_not_bias: The participant provides a qualified account of path dependence in information order and does not claim that the correct cause had been obvious at the time. This is not hindsight bias.

causal_claims.claim: The overnight bath-temperature spike was causing the pitting.
supporting_evidence: Night-shift handoff report of a temperature spike
Temperature is described as a classic anodizing-pitting contributor
Pitting dropped after the chiller was fixed and temperatures stabilized
causal_claims.audit: The evidence supports temperature as a plausible partial contributor but not as a demonstrated sole cause. Persistent pitting after temperature stabilization directly limits the original causal claim.

supporting_evidence: Residual pitting persisted after temperature stabilization
The residual defect pattern was interpreted as resembling chemistry-consistency variation
causal_claims.audit: This is a plausible diagnostic hypothesis, not an established causal conclusion. The transcript does not provide chemical assay results, controlled dosing data, rectifier exclusion evidence, or material evidence sufficient to isolate chemistry as the residual cause.

causal_claims.claim: Manual rectifier-voltage adjustments caused most of the turnaround.
supporting_evidence: The participant made manual voltage adjustments between runs
causal_claims.audit: Causally weak. The clean-batch period also included a recent retrofit and a routine bath-chemistry replenishment, and the participant confirms that these influences were not separated.

causal_claims.claim: The final clean lot was the truest picture of current process performance.
supporting_evidence: It was run immediately before PPAP submission
causal_claims.audit: The claim overstates what a single recent lot can establish. A defensible current-state conclusion should integrate the final lot with prior lot variability, process-capability evidence, sample adequacy, and evidence that the final lot was representative of normal operating conditions.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Temperature stabilization and reduced pitting occurred in temporal proximity.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: The reduction is consistent with temperature being contributory but cannot isolate the temperature effect from other changes, batch variation, or regression toward a lower observed defect rate.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Five clean batches followed retrofit installation, manual voltage adjustments, and chemistry replenishment.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: These concurrent changes create causal confounding. Chronological succession does not identify which factor, if any, produced the improvement.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: Day-shift defects coincided with a newer operator who was seen rushing rack loading.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: The association is compatible with an operator contribution but does not distinguish personal behavior from shift-time equipment condition, chemistry drift, material sequence, workload, supervision, or maintenance timing.

correlation_causation_risks.risk: A clean final validation lot immediately preceded PPAP certification recommendation.
correlation_causation_risks.why_it_matters: A favorable final observation may be relevant but cannot, by itself, establish sustained capability when the broader dataset contains variability and a marginal Cpk finding.

causal_audit.changed_variable: Order in which initial diagnostic evidence is reviewed: the operator's temperature-spike report first versus the rectifier calibration-deviation information first.
held_constant: Underlying true root cause or causes of the micro-pitting defect
Deadline pressure and PPAP audit timing
Vendor options and their documentation quality
Batch outcome sequence during trial runs
causal_audit.explanation: The counterfactual changes one cognitively relevant variable: the order in which competing diagnostic evidence is encountered and attended to. The participant's response is appropriately qualified, stating that the alternative order would probably have changed investigation priority without claiming it would have established a different physical root cause. The counterfactual remains coherent because it preserves the occupational context and does not introduce a second causal change. Although the interview is not a fully paired scenario, its hypothetical logic aligns with the specified information-order manipulation.

global_revision_constraints: No revision is required for manifest compliance.
If future versions are tuned for greater subtlety, preserve the current evidentiary distinctions rather than removing the explicit mechanism cues that make the occurrences auditable.
Maintain the distinction between process-state uncertainty and the participant's compensatory interpretation of the batch sequence.
Maintain the distinction between Vendor B ambiguity avoidance and Vendor A social-adoption weighting.
Maintain the distinction between initial diagnostic evidence order and personnel-performance attribution at decision point 1.
